For two molecules or atoms to react, they mustﬁrst move towards each other
and then, upon meeting, form new chemical bonds. Ultrafast spectroscopy
and diffraction techniques have illuminated the bond-formation step for
example by triggering reactions from weakly-bound precursors but not the
initial approach, typically attributed todiffusion, although this is often the step
that determines the reaction rate. Here, we measure and control the diffusion
time for the reaction where a Li⁺ ion forms a complex with a benzene dimer, a
textbook cation-π system, inside a liquid helium nanodroplet. Using
femtosecond-timed Coulomb explosion, weﬁnd that Li⁺, initially at the droplet
surface over 30 Å from the dimer, ﬁrst solvates, then diffuses ballistically at
43 m/s andﬁnally reacts. These results, rationalized by ring-polymer molecular
dynamics simulations, pave the way for real-time imaging of stereodynamics in
ion-molecule reactions.
Unimolecular processes such as bond-breaking and isomerization start
from the well-deﬁned geometry of a single parent molecule. Therefore,
their kinetics and even the changing molecular structure are, in prin-
ciple, straightforward to explore on the natural atomic time scale using
femtosecond (fs) pump-probe methods. This is not the case for a
bimolecular reaction between two atomic or molecular reactants A
and B, because such a process requires that A and Bﬁrst meet. In gases
and liquids, this happens via diffusion, and since the distance between
reactants varies, so does the moment they meet for any de ﬁned
starting time. Consequently, diffusion prevents the femtosecond time
resolution needed to follow the part of the reaction where chemical
bonds actually change. In certain cases, this timing problem may be
overcome if a weakly-bound, non-reactive A-B complex can be created
and if a fs pump pulse can initiate the bimolecular reaction by pho-
toexciting A or B
1–3. Such a precursor complex eliminates diffusion and
essentially turns the bimolecular reaction into a unimolecular process.
Examples in gas phase and solvents have been reported, including
proton transfer, vibrational dynamics and bond shortening
4–8.A n o t h e r
approach, demonstrated for radical-molecule and photo-redox reac-
tions in a solvent, is to increase the reactant concentration so much
that the diffusion time becomes almost negligible
9,10. It has also been
shown that the intrinsic rate constant of e.g. bimolecular electron
transfer reactions in solution can be determined when theoretical
modelling of diffusion is applied to fs time-resolved experimental
signals
11.
Under most synthetic or natural conditions, the two reactants are,
however, not in a close-proximity, precursor geometry. Rather, they
are brought together via diffusion, which for many reaction types
determines the overall reaction rate and may involve stereodynamical
effects as the reactants approach each other. Insight into the pro-
gression of the entire bimolecular reaction therefore requires time-
resolved techniques that also capture and possibly control the diffu-
sion stage, a so far unmet challenge. Here, we introduce an experi-
mental method that enables us to prepare two reactants, an ion and a
molecule, at a controllable initial distance, large enough that diffusion
must occur before they meet and react. The separation of the reactants

diffusion of the Li + ion in the He droplet is two orders of magnitude
faster. This difference reﬂects two qualitatively different types of dif-
fusion. In classical liquids, diffusion arises from Brownian motion, with
diffusion time proportional to the mean square displacement 26.I n
contrast, Li+ moves with constant velocity through the droplet, and
diffusion time depends linearly on distance, see Eq. ( 3). The linear
motion is an example of anomalous diffusion termed ballistic

27–29, a phenomenon also encountered under widely different
conditions, for instance in the transport of molecules in DNA model
condensates
30.
Currently, the time resolution of our technique is insuf ﬁcient to
capture details of the part of the reaction where new molecular
bonds form. To explore this, it may be favourable to start from
close-proximity precursor complexes. Helium droplets offer
opportunities in this regard by enabling formation of diverse
molecular and atomic complexes
31,32, going beyond what can be
accomplished using gas-phase samples or molecules in classical
solvents. Starting from a close-proximity precursor misses, how-
ever, the stereodynamics of reactions, i.e., as two reactants
approach, their mutual interaction may steer their relative
orientation into a particular reaction geometry
33–36. To explore this
fundamental aspect of bimolecular reactions, the two reactants
should start far apart, as ensured by the present method. In this
connection, we point out that stereodynamics of bimolecular reac-
tions have been explored extensively using crossed molecular
beams
37,38. In those works, typically addressing inelastic or reactive
scattering between an atom and a molecule, the molecule was
aligned or oriented along a laboratory- ﬁxed axis by a static electric
ﬁeld sometimes preceded by quantum-state-selection or photo-
selection. Varying the molecular orientation or alignment with
respect to the direction of the incoming atom and recording the
total or differential cross section have provided deep insight into
how steric effects in ﬂuence chemical reactions.
Our method can address stereodynamics in two fundamentally
different ways. Firstly, the molecule is not aligned or oriented by an
external ﬁeld de ﬁned in the laboratory frame. Instead, it is the
approaching ion that induces alignment or orientation of the molecule
through the interaction between its electrical properties and the
electric ﬁeld from the cation, see Supplementary Video 2. Secondly,
our experimental method is time-resolved. In the Li
+–Bz2 reaction, Bz2
gradually aligns the normal of its plane towards the trajectory of the
incoming Li+ ion, (Supplementary Information). Since it has already
been demonstrated that laser-induced Coulomb explosion can deter-
mine structure and alignment of molecules and molecular complexes
inside He droplets
39,40, we believe that our technique can be extended
to provide real-time imaging of stereodynamics in ion-molecule
reactions

In conclusion, we have introduced an experimental method to
explore, in real time, the bimolecular reaction where a Li+ ion diffuses
towards a benzene dimer and forms a Li +Bz2 complex inside a liquid
helium nanodroplet. In combination with atomistic RPMD simulations,
the experimental results allow us to draw a picture of the progression
of the entire reaction summarized in Fig. 4.T h eL i
+Bz2 complex is an
example of an ion-molecule system held together by noncovalent
bonding referred to as cation-π interaction
45. This interaction, which
has not been explored previously by fs time-resolved techniques, plays
an important role for e.g., molecular recognition in biological systems
and in organic synthesis
46. One opportunity opened by our work is to
measure the stereodynamics of the approaching reactants using timed
Coulomb explosion imaging. This should be possible for a variety of
molecules reacting with atomic or molecular ions of alkali and alkaline
earth atoms. Another opportunity is to explore interactions between
alkali atoms or dimers at the droplet surface and fullerenes in the
interior. The current method may provide insight into electron trans-
fer in such systems – recently explored by electron ionization mass
spectrometry
47, helium density functional theory 48 and path-integral
molecular dynamics simulations49,50.
Methods
Experimental details
An illustration of the experimental setup is shown in Supplementary
Information. More details can be found in Ref. 19. A beam of liquid
helium droplets is formed by subcritical expansion of 99.9999% purity
4He gas into vacuum through a 5 µm diameter ori ﬁce. The backing
pressure of the He gas was 50 bar in all experiments, while the tem-
perature of the expansion nozzle was varied between 13.5 K –20.5 K.
The resulting droplet distributions had an average number of helium
atoms between 3200 and 14600. The formed helium droplet beam
passes through two doping cells. Theﬁrst contains a vapor of benzene
molecules, let into the cell through a leak valve. The second contains a
gas of Li atoms obtained by heating a sample of solid Li in an oven. The

Suppl. Note 2.  Linear diffusion – the role of the helium solvent 
Based on the RPMD simulations, the motion of the Li+ ion can be divided into three steps: an 
initial acceleration and deceleration crossing the droplet surface, a drift region of constant 
velocity and finally an accelerated approach and reaction with the Bz 2 dimer. In this section, 
we discuss some details about these steps. 
When Li + is formed, its electric field polarizes the He atoms in the droplet. The resulting 
polarizability interaction between the electric field of Li + and the induced dipole moments in 
the helium atoms initially accelerate the ion into the droplet, as shown in Fig. 1b and Fig. 1e. 
These panels also show that after a few ps, the acceleration turns into deceleration, i.e. the ion 
feels friction from the droplet. T he friction may partly be due to the distortion of the droplet 
resulting from the energy that dissipates from the local region of Li + as it binds to the 
surrounding He atoms (6). The combination of acceleration and deceleration gives the Li+ ion 
a starting velocity towards the droplet center.  
After entering the droplet, the Li + ion begins the second step, where it moves with a constant 
velocity according to our RPMD simulations. For the trajectory depicted in Fig. 1a , the linear 
diffusion occurs from r(Li+−Bz2) ~ 22 Å (t = 10 ps) to ~ 13 Å (t = 45 ps). The Li+ ion must also 
be attracted to the Bz 2 dimer through the polarizability interaction, and to gauge the strength 
of this, we have repeated the RPMD simulation with the same starting configuration as for Fig.

1, but without the presence of helium. The resulting time dependences of r (Li+−Bz2) and 
r(Bz−Bz) are presented in Supplementary Fig 5. The panel clearly shows a non- zero 
acceleration, and that the Li + ion reaches the Bz 2 dimer faster than it would with the droplet 
present, see Fig. 1b and 1c. Thereby, the helium must provide a drag on the ion that counteracts 
the attraction to the benzene dimer. We note that while the simulation shows a constant 
diffusion velocity, it does not investigate whether this velocity is droplet size dependent or not. 
In principle, the simulations could be extended to larger droplet sizes, but doing so is currently 
not computationally feasible.  
For r(Li
+−Bz2) ~ 13 Å, the polarizability interaction has increased to a level  that perturbs the 
linear diffusion and accelerates the Li+ ion towards Bz2 such that the Li+Bz2 complex can form 
in the third step. We point out three key differences between the results of Supplementary Fig. 
5 and Fig. 1: (i) there is no strong drop during the first few ps in r(Li+−Bz2) for Supplementary 
Fig. 5 compared to Fig. 1b. We ascribe this to the lack of attraction between the newly formed 
Li+ ion and the helium atoms in the droplet. (ii) There is no region where r(Li+−Bz2) decreases 
linearly with time. Rather , its rate increases in the characteristic manner expected for the 
Li+−Bz2 polarizability interaction, which scale s as r(Li+−Bz2)-4. We ascribe this qualitatively 
different motion to the lack of friction on Li + from the helium solvent. (iii) Bz2 appears more 
fragile than in the helium droplet environment: one Bz molecule is being pulled away towards 
the approaching Li+ cation, before the Li+Bz complex turns around to form the Li+Bz2 complex 
in the more stable, sandwich configuration. Since there is no dissipative surrounding to 
accommodate the binding energy of the complex, Li +Bz2 will have an internal  energy 
exceeding the binding energy, making it likely to dissociate at longer times. 
We point out that superfluidity, normally characterizing helium nanodroplets, is not included 
in the simulations. As such, we expect the diffusion velocity determined from the simulation 
to underestimate the experimentally found 〈v

To prove that Li +Bz ions can only be produced when Li + has moved close enough to Bz 2, 
additional electronic structure calculations were performed for various configurations along 
the reaction pathway in the dicationic state. To produce the reactive trajectories, smaller 
droplets with He1800 were used with the orientation  angle θ at the time of ionization being

the strongly anisotropic interaction between Li + and the Bz molecules, as shown in 
Supplementary Fig. 6 for four selected trajectories with θ0 = 0°, 30°, 60°, and 90°, respectively. 
Several configurations of the  Li+Bz2 subsystem were then taken from the trajectories  at the 
centroids of the ring polymers for Li+Bz2 distances varying from about 25 Å to the final value 
of 3.2 Å  in the formed complex. For these configurations, single -point electronic structure 
calculations were conducted for the doubly cationic state with  three methods, namely MP2, 
DFT with the wB97xD functional and coupled cluster at the CCD level, all using the aug- cc-
pVDZ basis set. The charges on Li + and on each Bz molecule were determined using two 
alternative methods, namely the restricted electrostatic potential fitting (RESP) approach based 
on electrostatic potential fitting already used to assign partial charges on the benzene molecules 
within the framework of the Amber model, but also the well -established NBO (natural bond 
orbitals) approach .  
The effective charges were further averaged over  the four trajectories for the MP2 and DFT 
methods, only one trajectory being processed with the more expensive CCD method. The 
resulting charges are represented in Supplementary Fig. 7 as a function of the Li+-Bz2 distance. 
Overall, the two definitions of charges agree well with one another for all three methods, Li+ 
exhibiting only a limited amount of charge transfer ( < 0.2e) once the complex  is formed, in 
agreement with the electronic structure calculations  performed to adjust the  Li+-Bz potential. 
All methods also concur in that the extra charge created by the probe ionization is rather evenly 
shared between the two Bz molecules in the weakly bound Bz 2 molecule distant from Li+.

which will repel Li+. Only once Li+ has been brought close enough to one Bz molecule, with a 
Li+-Bz2 distance lower than 10 Å, does the extra charge become more strongly localized on the 
Bz molecule that is the most distant from the Li + ion. As the reaction proceeds with the Li +-
Bz2 distance decreasing below 8 Å and the complex approaching formation, ionization by the 
probe laser leads to a Li+Bz complex together with the other Bz molecule being ionized.

Suppl. Note 7. Stereodynamical effects in the Li+ + Bz2 → Li+Bz2 reaction 
An important aspect of many bimolecular reactions is stereodynamics. This is also true for the 
Li+ + Bz2 → Li+Bz2 reaction, exemplified by the anisotropic potentials between Li+ and Bz, as 
shown in Supplementary Fig. 2. It is energetically favorable for Li+ to bind to Bz along the 
normal of the molecular plane, and it is expected that the electric field of the ion will reorient 
the molecule such that this is the case. Fig. 1a is useful for illustrating the trajectory of the Li+ 
as it solvates and diffuses t owards the center of the droplet, but the stereodynamics are 
neglected as Bz2 is initially oriented in the configuration that minimizes the Li+-Bz2 interaction, 
chosen for computational considerations. To show the importance of the stereodynamics, we 
repeated the RPMD simulations for an 1800 -atom helium droplet, where 𝜃𝜃0 = 90° i.e. where 
the angle between the normal of the planes of the Bz 2 molecule and the Li +-Bz axis are 
perpendicular. Illustrations of the simulation are shown in Supplementary Fig. 8, while the 
movie can be seen in Supplementary Video 2. The panels clearly show that as the Li+ ion moves 
towards the center of the droplet where Bz2 is located, the dimer rotates such that the planes of 
the benzene molecules align to the trajectory of Li+. It is also only after the reorientation of the 
Bz2 molecule has taken place that the reaction occurs. Similar simulations have been done for 
the Li+ + Bz → Li+Bz reaction, where benzene also reorients itself as Li+ moves towards it for 
the case where 𝜃𝜃0 = 90°. We expect that the structural information obtainable with Coulomb 
explosion imaging can illuminate the rotation of the molecule of interest, if appropriate atomic 
substituents are used.

We fully agree that past work on stereodynamics of bimolecular reactions and scattering using

We agree that the benzene dimer may not initially be located in the center of the droplets. The

manuscript, the larger droplets show a deviation in ttotal from the linear diffusion regime. We

attribute this discrepancy to the delocalization of the Bz2 molecule; in the text (p. 7 l. 33-36). We 
have revised this sentence and added 64 words to fully cover this. 
Regarding the possibility of Li+ and Bz2 not reacting; we do not think this happens. If the dimer 
happens to be significantly away from the droplet center, the ion may miss it on the first passage of 
the center but the attraction between Li+ and Bz2 will bring them together later and lead to 
formation of the Li+Bz2 complex. If we assume that a substantial part of the droplet size

2) Intermolecular interactions. 
As an addition, it would be recommendable to dissect the physical contributions of the different pair 
interactions using Symmetry Adapted Perturbation Theory, which is implemented in open-access 
quantum-chemistry (QC) packages. In particular, it would allow to establish a correlation between

Authors response 
The regime where dispersion forces dominate is actually the one before the lithium atom is ionized, 
i.e. a regime where the reaction cannot take place because the two partners are separated from each 
other and barely interact. Once the lithium atom is ionized, it is polarization forces that cause the 
cation to enter the droplet, become solvated and then diffuse. This also happens without benzene 
molecules in the center. The interaction with the benzene molecules is also important, as they will 
of course trigger the formation of the complex at some later stage. We agree with the reviewer that 
it is interesting to distinguish the different contributions to the interaction energy in this case and 
when revisiting the Li+-benzene interaction potential (see below), we have now quantified the 
magnitude of the non-electrostatic contribution. 
 
The results obtained by partitioning the interaction energy clearly show that the electrostatic 
component (point charge-quadrupole) is essential in explaining why the cation-π complex is so 
stable as the cation approaches the benzene dimer along the reaction coordinate, perpendicular to 
the dimer plane. Parallel interactions, on the other hand, barely exhibit any contribution of the 
charge-quadrupole term, as expected.

Authors response  
The interaction between neutral Li and the benzene dimer is extremely weak at the long distances 
relevant prior to ionization. The interaction at arbitrary ranges is more complex but not of interest in 
our work because we only consider the Li atom at the droplet surface where it is very far (tens of Å) 
from the benzene dimer.  The Lennard-Jones form that we chose is consistent with the main 
interaction in the systems, which are also of the LJ form (especially among helium atoms), but 
should only be considered as a compromise between computational efficiency and chemical 
accuracy. The CCSD(T) calculations that we performed were limited to the long-range region as 
well - that is, for distances above 10 Å. The few points selected along the Z and X axes were used 
to fit the parameters of the LJ potential between Li and C and H atoms of the benzene monomer, in 
the region well above the equilibrium distance of a few Å.
